summary: Defines a RELOAD usage for application-layer multicast (ALM), so peer-to-peer overlays can distribute data to groups of receivers without network-level multicast. It aims to support different ALM control algorithms independent of the overlay, and gives two examples based on Scribe and P2PCast. It is experimental and came from a research group.

eli5.summary: Instead of the post office delivering one copy to everyone, friends pass the message along to each other until the whole group has it.

subtitle: Using peer-to-peer overlays to distribute data to groups without network multicast.

tldr.problem: Applications want to send messages to groups of receivers, but many networks lack native multicast support. Building application-level multicast on each platform separately wastes effort.
tldr.mechanism: RELOAD ALM defines messages and algorithms (Scribe, P2PCast) that layer multicast trees on top of RELOAD peer-to-peer overlays, letting different algorithms coexist in the same overlay.
tldr.outcome: Experimental research contribution. Scribe-style tree formation works well for some deployments; P2PCast addresses load balancing. Neither has seen widespread adoption.

facts.label: Message types defined
facts.value: 19 (Create, Join, Leave, Reform, Heartbeat, NodeQuery, Push, and their responses)

today: RFC 7019 is an Experimental protocol from the Internet Research Task Force. It has not been obsoleted or updated. RELOAD itself became a defined protocol (RFC 6940), and ALM remains a research contribution showing how to add multicast to peer-to-peer systems without network-layer support.

sections.title: What is Application-Layer Multicast?
sections.content:
Application-Layer Multicast (ALM) is a way for a group of peers to share data without help from the network routers. Instead, the application itself builds a tree of peer-to-peer connections and forwards messages along the tree. This is useful where native IP multicast is not available.

RFC 7019 defines how to do this using RELOAD, a structured peer-to-peer overlay protocol. It specifies messages for creating trees, joining and leaving groups, and forwarding data—independent of the exact tree-building algorithm. Two example algorithms (Scribe and P2PCast) show how different strategies can coexist.
sections.eli5: Instead of the post office running multicast, friends text each other about who is in the group and pass messages down a chain.

sections.title: How ALM Extends RELOAD
sections.content:
RELOAD is a distributed hash table (DHT) overlay where peers route messages to one another via the overlay network. RFC 7019 adds ALM on top by introducing an ALM Usage—a plugin that manages tree state and delegates to algorithm-specific modules (e.g., Scribe or P2PCast). The ALM component uses RELOAD's message transport to send control messages and data.

The architecture isolates algorithm choice from the overlay. All peers in a given tree use the same algorithm, but the overlay can host many trees using different algorithms at once. Tree metadata (root peer, group ID, configuration options) is stored in the DHT under a well-known resource name derived from a session key.
sections.eli5: RELOAD is the road network; ALM is the rule for which friend forwards a message to which other friends. You can run different rules on different friend groups at the same time.

sections.title: Tree Lifecycle Messages
sections.content:
ALM operations (create, join, leave, reform, heartbeat) are expressed as overlay messages routed through RELOAD. A peer wanting to create a tree sends a CreateALMTree message toward a peer responsible for the group ID in the overlay ID space. That peer stores tree metadata and becomes the tree root. New peers send Join requests toward the root; intermediate peers can accept them as children. Peers send JoinConfirm to confirm their parent choice, and Leave to detach.

The RFC defines 19 message types (includes responses and ancillary messages like Heartbeat to detect dead links and Reform to reorganize the tree). All messages use RELOAD's experimental message type and carry an algorithm ID so routers know which algorithm the tree uses.
sections.eli5: Friends send request cards: 'I want to join this group' (Join), 'I accept you as my parent' (JoinConfirm), 'Check that I'm still here' (Heartbeat), and 'Let's rearrange to be more efficient' (Reform).

sections.title: Scribe Tree Construction
sections.content:
Scribe (one of two example algorithms) creates a single tree rooted at the peer whose overlay ID is nearest to the group ID. Peers join by sending a request toward the root; intermediate peers on the path become forwarders if they are not yet in the tree. Data flows from any source down to the root and then down the tree to all peers.

The RFC extends Scribe with explicit JoinConfirm messages (a separate handshake step not in the original Scribe protocol) to allow peers to select among multiple candidate parents and to confirm their choice before committing to tree state.
sections.eli5: Friends find the nearest friend to the group's ID, make that the root, and when you join, you become a forwarder to your younger siblings in the ID space. Data goes up to the root, then down to everyone.

sections.title: P2PCast Load Balancing
sections.content:
P2PCast (the second example) splits incoming data into multiple stripes (e.g., two), creates a separate tree for each stripe, and requires every peer to be an internal node in exactly one tree and a leaf in all others. This distributes upload burden evenly: peers receive from one parent per stripe and send to multiple children in one tree.

P2PCast nodes are typed: incomplete (fewer children than stripes), complete (exactly as many), leaf (none), or special (leaf in all trees). Join logic routes a new peer to different positions in each stripe based on node types, keeping trees balanced.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big tree, split the stream into two parts. Every friend carries one part and receives the other, so no one is overloaded.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC assumes node authentication and security associations as provided by base RELOAD (RFC 5213). It highlights security issues specific to ALM: controlling who can create a group at a given ID, who can store tree metadata in the DHT, limiting message rates and bandwidth per peer, and controlling access to join specific groups. It does not solve overlay-level DoS or collusion attacks—those are assumed to be handled at the RELOAD layer.
sections.eli5: You need to know your friends won't cheat, and RELOAD already checks that. This doc flags that some friends shouldn't be allowed to make groups or join trees they don't belong to.
